name: ai.rakelabs/rake-mcp
title: Rake
description: Write and debug firmware with exact chip data

tools.name: find_device
tools.description: Says what data the server has for a part name: the device with register data, the vector table and the pin data, and the exact names to use in the other tools. Use it first when a part number is loose or partial, such as "stm32g431" or "nrf5340", or to see whether a part is covered at all. Register data covers ST, Nordic, Raspberry Pi, Espressif, Microchip, NXP and TI parts, vector tables ST parts and pin data ST parts.

name.description: A part number or the start of one, for example STM32F407VGT6, stm32g431, nRF52840 or esp32-c3.

tools.name: lookup_register
tools.description: Returns the address, size, access, reset value and bit fields of a register of a microcontroller, or the registers of a peripheral, from the vendor's own file for the part. Use it instead of recalling a register address, a bit position or a field name from memory, and to find what an address in a fault report or a debugger belongs to. Covers 935 devices from ST, Nordic, Raspberry Pi, Espressif, Microchip, NXP and TI, and says so when it has no data for a part.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F407VGT6, stm32g431, nrf52840 or esp32c3.

name.description: What to look up: a register (USART1->BRR), a field (RCC->APB2ENR.USART1EN or RCC_APB2ENR_USART1EN), a peripheral alone (GPIOA) to list its registers, an address (0x40011008), or a register or a bit that the code names alone (TCCR1B, CS12).

tools.name: check_registers
tools.description: Checks a list of register, field and peripheral names against the vendor's own file for a microcontroller and says for each whether it exists, with its address or bit position, or names the closest that do. Use it after writing or reviewing register-level code, on every name the code uses, to catch a register or bit that does not exist on this part. Covers 935 devices from ST, Nordic, Raspberry Pi, Espressif, Microchip, NXP and TI, and says so when it has no data for a part. Names follow that file. Another file of the vendor, such as a header, can spell a few of them differently.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F407VGT6, stm32g431, nrf52840 or esp32c3.

names.description: The names as the code has them: USART1->BRR, RCC->APB2ENR.USART1EN, RCC_APB2ENR_USART1EN, GPIOA->MODER, P0->PIN_CNF[3], TCCR1B, CS12.

tools.name: decode_registers
tools.description: Decodes a register dump of a microcontroller into registers and bit fields, with the named value of each field, from the vendor's own file for the part. With a second dump it returns only what differs between the two. Use it to see what a peripheral is really set to, and to compare a setup that works with one that does not: a vendor example against your code, or a good board against a bad one. A dump is a read: on some status and data registers a read clears flags or takes a byte. Covers 935 devices from ST, Nordic, Raspberry Pi, Espressif, Microchip, NXP and TI, and says so when it has no data for a part.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F407VGT6, stm32g431, nrf52840 or esp32c3.

dump.description: The dump, in 32-bit words: lines as GDB prints them for `x/16xw 0x40011000`, as OpenOCD prints them for `mdw`, or lines of the form `USART1->CR1 = 0x200C`.

compare.description: A second dump of the same registers, for example from the setup that fails. The answer then holds only the differences, as first -> second.

tools.name: list_interrupts
tools.description: Returns the interrupt numbers and names of a microcontroller and, where the data has the vendor's device header, the handler names of the startup file. Use it to find the interrupt number for a call that enables or prioritises it, the exact handler name to define, or which peripherals share a vector. Handler names come from device headers, which the data has for ST parts. For other parts the list comes from the file that the registers come from, without handler names.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F103C8T6, STM32G431KB, nrf52840 or rp2040.

filter.description: Only interrupts whose name or description holds this text, for example USART or DMA. Omit for all.

tools.name: check_interrupt_handlers
tools.description: Checks interrupt handler function names against the vector table of a part and says for each whether the startup file declares it, or names the closest that it does. Use it on every interrupt handler function in the code: a handler with a name the startup file does not declare compiles and links, and is never called. It needs the vendor's device header, which the data has for ST parts. For another part it says so and judges nothing.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F103C8T6 or STM32G431KB.

names.description: The handler function names, for example USART1_IRQHandler, TIM1_UP_TIM10_IRQHandler, HardFault_Handler.

tools.name: find_pins
tools.description: Returns the pins of a part that can carry a signal, with what the code must select to route it there, such as the alternate function, or every signal of one pin. Use it to pick the pin for a peripheral signal such as USART2_TX, to get the alternate function number for it, or to see what else a pin can do. Pin data comes from the vendors' own pin files, which the data has for ST parts, per package. For another part it says so.

part.description: The part number. With the package, as in STM32F407VGT6, the answer is for that package. Without it, as in STM32F407VG, for every package.

signal.description: A signal as the vendor names it: USART2_TX, I2C1_SCL, TIM3_CH1, SPI1_MOSI, ADC1_IN5.

pin.description: A pin, for example PA9. Give this or a signal.

tools.name: calc_can_bit_timing
tools.description: Computes the CAN bit timing for a clock, a bit rate and a sample point: prescaler, time quanta, both segments and the jump width, with the real bit rate, the real sample point and the register value. Use it when setting up CAN or CAN FD instead of working the values out by hand. The controller classic gives the counts for a classic CAN controller whose time quantum is the prescaler times the clock period, within the fields most of them have: a prescaler up to 64, segments up to 16 and 8 quanta, and a jump width up to 4. sja1000 and mcp2515 are those two controllers, which halve the oscillator before the prescaler and have limits of their own. With bxcan (CAN_BTR of STM32) or mcan-nominal and mcan-data (NBTP and DBTP of Bosch M_CAN, which several vendors use for CAN FD), it also packs the register value.

controller.description: classic (counts only, a plain prescaler), sja1000 or mcp2515 (counts only), bxcan, mcan-nominal (arbitration phase) or mcan-data (the data phase of CAN FD).

clock_hz.description: The clock that feeds the bit timing logic of the CAN controller, in Hz. It is often not the core clock. For sja1000 and mcp2515, the frequency of the oscillator.

bit_rate.description: The bit rate in bits per second, for example 500000. Above 1000000 only for mcan-data.

sample_point.description: The wanted sample point as a fraction of the bit. Default 0.875, which CANopen and DeviceNet use.

tools.name: calc_uart_baud
tools.description: Computes the divisor for a UART baud rate from the peripheral clock, with the real baud rate and its error in percent, and the BRR value for STM32. Use it to set a baud rate or to find out why a link shows framing errors or garbage. The peripheral generic fits any UART that divides its clock by a whole number, with 16 or 8 samples a bit. For the STM32 USART and LPUART it also gives the BRR value.

clock_hz.description: The clock of the UART in Hz.

oversampling.description: Samples per bit, 16 or 8. Default 16. The LPUART ignores it.

tools.name: calc_timer_prescaler
tools.description: Computes the prescaler and the auto-reload value of a timer for an update or PWM frequency, with the real frequency, its error and the PWM duty resolution in bits. Use it to set up a periodic interrupt or a PWM output. For any timer with a 16-bit prescaler and a 16-bit or 32-bit counter that both count from 0, which is how most microcontroller timers are built.

clock_hz.description: The clock of the timer in Hz, which is often not the bus clock: check the clock tree of the part.

frequency_hz.description: The wanted update or PWM frequency in Hz. Fractions are allowed, such as 0.5.

counter_bits.description: The width of the counter, 16 or 32. Default 16.

tools.name: calc_i2c_timing
tools.description: Computes I2C timing from the limits of the I2C-bus specification: the SCL low and high times for a bus speed as counts of the controller's clock, or the register value of a controller it knows. It can also check an existing register value against the limits. Use it to set up an I2C controller instead of copying a timing value from another project, where the clock differs. The controller generic gives counts for any controller that takes SCL low and high times. The controller stm32-timingr gives I2C_TIMINGR for the STM32 series that have that register, which F1, F2, F4 and L1 do not.

controller.description: generic for counts of the controller's clock, or stm32-timingr for the STM32 I2C_TIMINGR register.

clock_hz.description: The clock of the I2C controller in Hz. For stm32-timingr, the I2C kernel clock selected in RCC.

mode.description: standard (up to 100 kHz), fast (up to 400 kHz) or fast-plus (up to 1 MHz).

bus_hz.description: The wanted SCL frequency in Hz. Default: the highest the mode allows.

rise_ns.description: The rise time of SCL and SDA in ns. Default: the longest the mode allows.

fall_ns.description: The fall time of SCL and SDA in ns. Default: the longest the mode allows.

analog_filter.description: stm32-timingr only: whether the analog noise filter is on. Default true, as after reset.

digital_filter.description: stm32-timingr only: the DNF field of I2C_CR1, 0 to 15. Default 0.

timingr.description: stm32-timingr only: an existing I2C_TIMINGR value to check. Omit it to compute one.

tools.name: calc_watchdog_timeout
tools.description: Computes the register values of a watchdog for a timeout, with the real timeout. Use it to set up a watchdog instead of working the prescaler and the reload value out by hand. It knows the STM32 independent watchdog (IWDG_PR and IWDG_RLR), the STM32 window watchdog (WDGTB and the counter) and the nRF watchdog (CRV). The timeout is never shorter than the one asked for.

clock_hz.description: The clock of the watchdog in Hz. Default 32000 for stm32-iwdg (LSI) and 32768 for nrf-wdt. Required for stm32-wwdg: its APB clock.

tools.name: decode_cortex_m_fault
tools.description: Decodes Arm Cortex-M fault status register values (CFSR, and optionally HFSR, MMFAR, BFAR, SFSR, SFAR, EXC_RETURN and the stacked PC) into the faults they record and the checks to make next. For Cortex-M3, M4, M7, M33, M55 and M85. Use it when firmware lands in HardFault, MemManage, BusFault, UsageFault or SecureFault and the register values are known.

cfsr.description: Configurable Fault Status Register, read from 0xE000ED28.

mmfar.description: MemManage Fault Address Register, read from 0xE000ED34.

sfsr.description: SecureFault Status Register, read from 0xE000EDE4. Cores with TrustZone only.

sfar.description: SecureFault Address Register, read from 0xE000EDE8. Cores with TrustZone only.

exc_return.description: The value of LR at the first instruction of the fault handler, 0xFFFFFFxx.

stacked_pc.description: The PC value in the exception stack frame.

tools.name: decode_riscv_trap
tools.description: Decodes the mcause value of a 32-bit RISC-V core into the exception or interrupt it names, and says what mepc and mtval hold for that cause and what to check. Use it when a RISC-V microcontroller, such as an ESP32-C3 or a GD32V, stops in its trap handler and the register values are known. It covers the causes of the RISC-V privileged specification, not vendor-specific ones.

mcause.description: The mcause register. Bit 31 set means an interrupt.

mepc.description: The mepc register: the program counter that the core saved when it took the trap.

mtval.description: The mtval register: the faulting address or instruction, depending on the cause.

tools.name: decode_esp_panic
tools.description: Reads the text an ESP32-family chip prints when ESP-IDF panics and returns the cause, what it means, what to check and the addresses to resolve. Use it when the serial output shows a Guru Meditation Error, an abort(), a task watchdog or interrupt watchdog timeout, a stack overflow or a brown-out. It handles the Xtensa chips and the RISC-V chips. It does not turn addresses into source lines: that needs the ELF file.

log.description: The serial output around the failure, as printed. Include the register dump and the backtrace where the output has them.

tools.name: decode_zephyr_fatal
tools.description: Reads the text Zephyr prints on a fatal error and returns the fault, the thread, the faulting address, what to check and the command that resolves the address. Use it when the console shows "ZEPHYR FATAL ERROR", a fault block such as "***** BUS FAULT *****" or "ASSERTION FAIL". The fault detail lines it reads are those of the Arm Cortex-M port. It does not turn addresses into source lines: that needs the ELF file.

log.description: The console output of the fatal error, as printed, from the fault lines to "Halting system".

tools.name: lookup_zephyr_kconfig
tools.description: Returns a Zephyr Kconfig symbol of a release: type, prompt, range, defaults, dependencies, what selects it and its help text. Or searches symbol names and prompts for words. Use it instead of recalling a CONFIG_ name or its meaning from memory, and to find the symbol for a feature. Covers the symbols of Zephyr 3.7, 4.4, 4.5 and of the modules in its manifest. It does not cover symbols that only the nRF Connect SDK or another downstream tree defines.

symbol.description: The symbol, with or without the CONFIG_ prefix, for example CONFIG_UART_INTERRUPT_DRIVEN.

search.description: Words to search for in symbol names and prompts, for example "uart interrupt". Give this or a symbol.

version.description: The Zephyr release: 3.7, 4.4, 4.5. Default 4.5. For another release, use the nearest one below it.

tools.name: check_zephyr_conf
tools.description: Checks the lines of a Zephyr configuration file (prj.conf, a board .conf or an overlay) against the Kconfig symbols of a release: symbols that do not exist, with the closest that do, values of the wrong type or outside the range, and symbols that a file cannot set. Use it after writing or editing a prj.conf, before building. It does not evaluate dependencies or board defaults, so the build can still warn about a symbol whose dependencies are not met.

conf.description: The text of the configuration file.

version.description: The Zephyr release: 3.7, 4.4, 4.5. Default 4.5. For another release, use the nearest one below it.

tools.name: lookup_zephyr_binding
tools.description: Returns the devicetree binding of a compatible in a Zephyr release: its properties with type, whether required, allowed values and defaults, the bus it sits on, its child nodes and its specifier cells. Use it when writing a devicetree node or overlay, instead of recalling property names from memory. Covers the bindings in the Zephyr tree for 3.7, 4.4, 4.5. Bindings that a module or an application adds are not covered.

compatible.description: The compatible string, for example st,stm32-uart, nordic,nrf-uarte, bosch,bme280 or gpio-leds. Words are searched when nothing matches.

version.description: The Zephyr release: 3.7, 4.4, 4.5. Default 4.5. For another release, use the nearest one below it.

tools.name: check_freertos_config
tools.description: Reads the content of a FreeRTOSConfig.h and reports settings that stop the build, break the kernel at run time or hide errors, with the values it read. Use it when a FreeRTOS project hangs in a critical section, hard-faults at the first context switch, or before trusting a configuration copied from another project. It checks the interrupt priorities of the Cortex-M ports, stack and heap failure detection, the tick settings, software timers and the hooks the application owes. It does not evaluate #if conditions.

config.description: The text of the FreeRTOSConfig.h file.

tools.name: check_esp_idf_api
tools.description: Finds the ESP-IDF functions, types and headers in a piece of code that do not fit the ESP-IDF release of the project: removed, changed or deprecated by that release, or introduced after it. Each finding names the replacement. Use it on ESP32 code before building, when the code may come from another ESP-IDF major version, for example ESP-IDF 4 driver calls in an ESP-IDF 5 project. The list comes from Espressif's migration guides for ESP-IDF 5.0 to 5.5, so a name outside those guides is not judged.

code.description: The C or C++ source to check.

idf_version.description: The ESP-IDF release the project builds with, for example 5.3 or 4.4.

tools.name: check_build_flags
tools.description: Reads compiler and linker command lines, or the values of CFLAGS and LDFLAGS, and reports what bites on a microcontroller: objects built for different cores or float ABIs, a link line without the core or the float ABI, sections without garbage collection, a build without debug information or without warnings. Use it after writing or changing a Makefile, a CMake toolchain file or the flags of a build. It knows the flags of GCC and Clang and reads the flags only, not the code.

flags.description: The command lines or lists of flags, one command per line: a compile line and the link line, or the values of CFLAGS and LDFLAGS.

tools.name: get_platform_pitfalls
tools.description: Returns the traps of one microcontroller family, RTOS, SDK or bus as habits: when something shows up there or before a risky step, what to do, and why. Use it before writing code for a platform or a bus that has not come up in this session, and when a board will not connect, flash or start. Subjects: buses, esp-idf, esp32, freertos, kinetis, nrf-connect, nrf52, pico-sdk, rp2040, samd, stm32, stm32-hal, zephyr. Omit the subject or the topic for the list.

subject.description: The family, RTOS, SDK or group of buses. Omit it for the list of subjects.

topic.description: One topic of the subject. Omit it for the list of topics.

tools.name: diagnose_symptom
tools.description: Returns what a firmware engineer does when a board shows a symptom: the order to work in, the suspects in order of likelihood, what to ask the board first, and what each answer means. Use it before changing code for anything seen on hardware: a hang, a reset, a fault that comes and goes, a silent bus, a build that works only with the debugger. With a device, it names the registers to read on that part. Omit the symptom for the list.

symptom.description: The symptom that fits what the board does. Omit it for the list with a line on each.

device.description: The part, for example STM32F407VG or nrf52840. The answer then names the registers to read on it.

tools.name: get_debug_technique
tools.description: Returns how to make firmware show what it does, on the bench or in the code and the build: watch a variable the optimiser removed, time a handler with a pin, keep evidence across a reset, find who corrupts memory, match a wire format, let the compiler forbid a mistake, shrink an image. Each move says what it shows and what it costs. Use it when you need an observation, or a compiler, linker or macro technique, instead of a guess. Omit the goal for the list.

goal.description: What you want to see or achieve. Omit it for the list with a line on each.

tools.name: get_playbook
tools.description: Returns the steps of a firmware task in the order that keeps every step provable: bringing up a new board, writing a driver, an interrupt handler, a watchdog, a firmware update, low power. Use it before starting one of these tasks. Each step says when it is done, and the next one stands on it. Omit the task for the list.

task.description: The task. Omit it for the list with a line on each.

tools.name: get_break_list
tools.description: Returns the faults to try on firmware, by area: power, buses, inputs, time, memory and storage, clocks, updates, the watchdog and missing parts, with the order to work through them. Use it to review or test firmware for robustness, one fault at a time. Omit the area for the list.

area.description: The area of faults. Omit it for the list with a line on each.

tools.name: get_firmware_rules
tools.description: Returns coding rules for microcontroller firmware in C, C++ or Rust. Each rule has an id, a habit with its reason, what to look for in review, and the MISRA or CERT rule numbers it relates to. The rules that block a change come first. Use it before writing firmware code, or to review code rule by rule, where a finding can name the id of its rule. Give a context to get only the rules for that kind of code.

language.description: The language of the code: c, cpp or rust.

context.description: The kind of code: bare-metal, rtos (task code), interrupt (handlers), driver or bootloader. Omit for every rule of the language.
